statement: Foetuses increase in weight proportional to cubed time.

scores.rationale: Multiple snippets directly support the stylized fact. Snippets [2], [3], [9], [10], and [16] explicitly state that foetal structural volume/weight is proportional to cubed time, derived as V(t) = (vt/3)^3 in the standard DEB model and originally observed empirically by Huggett and Widdas (1951). Snippet [1] supports the consistency of this with the DEB model (weight doubling times increasing by factor 2^(1/3)). A few snippets ([13], [14]) instead assume exponential foetal growth, but these are simplified modeling choices in specific marine-mammal applications rather than evidence against the cubic relationship; note snippet [17] shows that under certain DEB conditions foetal length can grow approximately linearly (consistent with the cubic-weight result). The remaining snippets are topically related but neutral. Overall there is strong, repeated, mutually consistent support for the cubic-time growth pattern with only minor, application-specific deviations.

scores.rationale: The stylized fact states foetal weight increases proportional to cubed time, which under DEB theory corresponds to the cube-root of weight being linear in time (W^(1/3) ∝ t). Snippet 12 uniquely expresses growth rates in g^(1/3)/d units, implying linear growth in cube-root of weight and thus weight proportional to cubed time, providing the only direct affirmative support. Snippet 16 shows increasing daily weight gains over gestation, weakly consistent with accelerating (cubic-like) growth. However, snippets 1 and 4 describe fetal growth as exponential in mid-gestation and linear in late gestation, which conflicts with a simple cubic-time model. The remaining snippets concern litter size, placental constraint, twin/triplet effects, and maternal condition, and are topically related but do not bear on the cubic-time pattern. Overall, evidence is sparse, with one clearly supporting reference (the g^(1/3) growth metric) but also conflicting characterizations, so support is weak and the direction is insufficiently determined.
